question: Is buy now, pay later actually free, or does it quietly drive people into debt?
rationale: Buy now, pay later apps like Klarna, Afterpay and Affirm are pitched at checkout as a free way to split any purchase into four payments, and finance creators on TikTok and YouTube, plus outlets like NPR and CBS, push back just as loudly that the loans push people into overspending, debt stacking and bank overdrafts. The CFPB, the Federal Reserve Board and the Kansas City Fed have each measured exactly how often BNPL use coincides with financial strain, missed payments and overdraft fees, and by how much more than non-users experience them.
fit: The Commission on Spending already asks whether a purchase anyone can make, a car, a heating system, a grocery basket, actually costs what it looks like at the register. Buy now, pay later is the payment method now offered at that same register, marketed as costing nothing extra, so it continues the channel's household-economics lens into how a purchase is financed rather than only what it is priced at. The claims split sharply between the apps and their critics, and government researchers have measured the gap directly.
claims: Buy now, pay later purchases feel free because they charge no interest.
Splitting a purchase into four payments makes shoppers buy more than they would upfront.
People who take out a BNPL loan every month carry more other debt than similar shoppers.
Missed BNPL payments trigger bank overdraft fees far more often for users than non-users.
BNPL loans stay invisible on credit reports, so other lenders can't see them.
Younger borrowers carry a much larger share of their debt in BNPL loans.
Most BNPL users who pay late were already financially stretched before borrowing.
Many shoppers run several BNPL loans across different apps at once.
A BNPL balance can be wiped out in bankruptcy just like any other unsecured debt.
Self-reported late payment rates run far higher than the delinquency rates lenders report.
Canceling buy now, pay later apps is becoming a deliberate budgeting move.
Retailers push BNPL at checkout because it increases the average order size.
